newsitem.title: HUNGARY: OECD says Hungary should tackle inflation, jobless.
newsitem.headline: OECD says Hungary should tackle inflation, jobless.

text.p: Two years of reforms have put Hungary on track to converge with Western Europe, but it still needs to beat high inflation and unemployment, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said.

"High inflation and unemployment indicate that the macroeconomic adjustment has further to go...while remaining impediments to longer-run growth are apparent in the problems of tax evasion and assessment of collateral," said an OECD report on Hungary, which joined the organisation last year.

The report said a credible monetary stance and firm fiscal policies since 1995 have helped Hungary significantly improve external and internal balances and lay the groundwork for renewed economic growth.

Though the steps led to a more than 10-percent drop in personal consumption up to the end of last year and a slowdown in gross domestic product (GDP) growth, they also produced a major transfer of income from labour to capital, the OECD said.
"This can be an example that short-term pains can bring gains for the longer-term," OECD Secretary General Donald Johnston told a news conference here.
The OECD forecasts 1997 GDP growth up at 2.5 percent and 3.5 percent in 1998 from a preliminary one percent in 1996.

But the report said growth in domestic sales and GDP will be slow this year. It also did not expect private consumption to increase by more than 1.5 percent over the next two years unless savings fall sharply, which would be unfavourable.
The OECD urged the government to increase its efforts in wage and price bargaining to reduce the high inflation rate, which distorts savings and investment decisions and hinders lending to companies.
"The government and central bank have set an inflation goal of 17 to 18 percent in 1997, which implies an only two-percentage point decline in December year-on-year inflation rates," it said.
In average terms, inflation could drop by some five percent from 1996 to 1997, and the country's inflation target for this year is likely to be met, an OECD official told Reuters.

"However, we cannot help but notice that most of that success occurred last year and in some respect, progress in 1997 will be relatively small," Andrew R. Burns, OECD's principal administrator for the Czech Republic and Hungary said.
He said Hungary could reach its 1998 average inflation target of 13.5 percent through an intensive process of bargaining with employers and employees.
"If the government achieves 13.5 percent next year, that will be a success very much," he said.

High inflation and a slow modernisation of the out-of-date property registry makes banks cautious in lending to companies though financial market reforms have made Hungary's banking system "perhaps the healthiest and most completely privatised" in the region, the OECD said.

But the report noted a number of Hungary's institutional structures were similar to ones in other European countries that have led to high structural unemployment. This means Hungary would need wage flexibility, job protection, education and technological innovation reforms.
Hungary's jobless rate is near 10 percent and can drop to nine percent in two years, the OECD said.

If inflation and wide-scale tax-evasion woes are tackled and pre-emptive labour market reforms are undertaken, Hungary can look move toward levels of development seen in Western Europe, the OECD said.
